topics.title: Chapter overview
topics.summary: A dependency slows down. Every caller retries immediately. A circuit breaker opens, then every instance probes recovery at the same instant. Meanwhile, a shared thread pool fills with waiting calls and unrelated requests stop progressing.

topics.title: 19.1.2 Combining Backoff, Jitter, and Remaining Time
topics.summary: Exponential backoff increases the delay ceiling as failures continue, up to a cap. Jitter spreads retry times so many clients do not remain synchronized. The companion uses a uniform delay between zero and the current capped ceiling for its teaching retry policy.

blocks.text: Backoff must fit within the operation’s remaining budget. If only 20 ms remains and the next delay alone is 100 ms, sleeping and then starting a doomed attempt wastes resources. Return the appropriate timeout or pending state instead. A background durable workflow can have a different recovery horizon, but it still needs a defined policy.

topics.title: 19.2.1 Defining Closed, Open, and Half-Open Behavior
topics.summary: A closed breaker admits calls and records relevant outcomes. An open breaker rejects or redirects new calls according to policy. After a cooldown, a half-open state admits a bounded probe to determine whether ordinary traffic should resume. These names are useful only when transitions and counted outcomes are specified.

blocks.text: The model counts consecutive failures until a threshold opens the breaker. It admits one half-open probe at a time. A successful probe closes the breaker; a failed probe reopens it. This is a deliberately small single-owner policy, not a thread-safe distributed health system.

blocks.text: Define which failures affect the breaker. A client-side validation error may say nothing about dependency health. A timeout caused by local queueing may require local capacity action rather than declaring the remote service broken. Counting every exception indiscriminately can open a breaker for reasons outside its intended scope.

topics.title: 19.2.2 Ignoring Completions from an Obsolete Breaker Epoch
topics.summary: Calls admitted before a breaker opens can complete afterward. If their successes blindly reset the breaker, an old result can close a newly opened state. The model attaches an epoch ticket to each admitted call and ignores completions from an older epoch.

topics.title: 19.3.1 Building Bulkheads Around Actual Scarce Resources
topics.summary: A bulkhead limits how much one class of work can consume so another class retains capacity. Separate worker pools, connection limits, queue capacities, or database budgets can implement it. The correct boundary depends on the scarce resource, not merely on service names.

blocks.text: The epoch ticket solves this local race by tying completion to the generation that admitted it. B’s result can still be recorded as a successful attempt for observability, but it cannot mutate the current breaker’s state when its ticket is obsolete. The business response and policy update are separate decisions.
